content:
BIOS: Restore on AC power loss = Power On; enable Wake-on-LAN. DHCP reservation for the server. Install the package, either from the apt repository (preferred, gives upgrades: see the apt repository page) or from a downloaded file: sudo apt install ./server-hands_X.Y.Z_amd64.deb sudo handsctl discover --write, then review labels and the [post_unlock] lists in /etc/server-hands/config.toml. Drives with an /etc/crypttab entry are skipped and reported. Add a phone-only keyslot per drive (you will be prompted for the existing passphrase; the new one is generated and shown once for entry into the app): sudo handsctl add-phone-key <luks-uuid> (libcryptsetup directly; the existing passphrase is read from the tty, nothing goes through argv) Post-unlock actions. Docker and the other services are not gated: they start at boot as usual. Containers that need the encrypted drives are started by scripts instead, so containers that only use the root disk are unaffected. Stop the dependent containers from starting at boot, so they do not come up on empty mount points: set restart: "no" in their compose files (or docker update --restart=no <container>) so the script is the only thing that starts them.
Put the commands in a script, e.g. start from /usr/share/server-hands/post-unlock-example.sh:
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/server-hands/scripts sudo install -m 0755 /usr/share/server-hands/post-unlock-example.sh /etc/server-hands/scripts/media.sh sudo nano /etc/server-hands/scripts/media.shIt must be owned by root and not writable by anyone else (its directory too), and must not be under /home. handsd refuses to run it otherwise.
Register it in /etc/server-hands/config.toml:
[[script]] name = "media" label = "Media containers" path = "/etc/server-hands/scripts/media.sh" mode = "auto" # runs right after the unlock; "manual" = only when you tap Run in the appManual scripts do not have to be about the unlock: add requires_unlock = false to one (a status check, a service restart, a reboot) and the app can run it at any time, even while the drives are locked. Without it a manual script is refused until every drive is unlocked.
For dangerous scripts (a reboot, say) add requires_confirmation = true (the app asks “Run X?”) or biometric_protection = true (the phone must produce a fresh fingerprint/face, which the server checks with a challenge it issues; the biometric prompt then replaces the dialog). The first protected run registers the phone’s approval key automatically. If the phone’s biometrics change, the key is destroyed; run sudo handsctl reset-approval-key <device-id> (ids from handsctl devices) and the phone registers a new one on its next protected run. Scripts run as root in a transient unit, in the order listed, after the pool is refreshed. A non-zero exit or the timeout_secs limit (default 300) shows as “failed” in the app. Output: journalctl -u server-hands-script-media.
Test it without a reboot: sudo systemctl restart handsd, unlock (or, with the drives already open, handsd runs auto scripts at startup), then check the app’s “Scripts” card.
The mergerfs pool: list its mount unit in mount_units. To get the value (run these with the drives unlocked and the pool mounted):
findmnt -t fuse.mergerfs -o TARGET,SOURCE # the pool's mount point, e.g. /srv/mergerfs/Pool systemd-escape --path --suffix=mount /srv/mergerfs/Pool # its unit name: srv-mergerfs-Pool.mount systemctl list-units --type=mount | grep -i mergerfs # confirm that unit existsIf findmnt prints nothing, the pool is not mounted; the pool’s name is on the OMV web UI’s Storage > Union Filesystems page, and the mount point is /srv/mergerfs/<name> (check with ls /srv/mergerfs). Then put the unit name in the config:
[post_unlock] mount_units = ["srv-mergerfs-Pool.mount"]The same list feeds the pool bar in the app, so a wrong name shows as “Not mounted” there. After the drives are mounted handsd runs systemctl restart on it, exactly as the OMV mergerfs plugin’s “restart pool” action does. If something holds the pool open (a running container or Samba), the restart can fail with “target is busy”; keep those out of boot, or start them from a script.
service_units takes plain systemd unit names (systemctl list-unit-files | grep -i smb finds them, e.g. smbd.service); they are started without waiting after the unlock. Prefer a script for containers.
Optional hard gating of a systemd service (the old approach): sudo install -D -m644 /usr/share/server-hands/gated-service.conf /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/server-hands.conf, add the unit to service_units.
sudo systemctl enable --now handsd.socket handsd.service, then run systemd-analyze security handsd.service and expect an exposure of 3.0 or lower. sudo handsctl pair, scan the QR in the app, confirm the 6-digit code on both sides. Shorter boot delay (optional, recommended). The locked drives’ fstab entries make systemd wait for their devices for the default 90 s before giving up, which stalls boot. Lower the default device timeout: sudo install -D -m644 /usr/share/server-hands/10-server-hands.conf /etc/systemd/system.conf.d/10-server-hands.conf sudo systemctl daemon-reexec # or just rebootThis sets DefaultDeviceTimeoutSec=10s in [Manager]. It is global (every device wait in fstab, also USB or network disks), so use a larger value if you have slow-appearing disks. OMV regenerates /etc/fstab, so per-entry x-systemd.device-timeout= options would be overwritten; the global setting survives. Check the effect after a reboot with systemd-analyze blame | head and systemd-analyze critical-chain. To undo: delete the file and systemctl daemon-reexec. Reboot, open the app, approve. Check the OMV GUI shows the drives unlocked and mounted. Recovery (lost phone): unlock in the OMV GUI with the human passphrase; sudo handsctl revoke <device>; cryptsetup luksKillSlot <dev> <slot>.
Troubleshooting a failing script The app only shows “failed”; the reason is in the server’s journal. Replace media with the script’s name:
# the script's own output and exit status journalctl -u server-hands-script-media -n 100 --no-pager # handsd's verdict ("script media ok/failed") and refusals journalctl -u handsd -n 50 --no-pager | grep -i scriptWhat “failed” can mean:
The script exited non-zero. The cause is in server-hands-script-<name>. The unit is transient and removed after it finishes, so use the journal rather than systemctl status. It hit timeout_secs (default 300). The unit’s journal shows it was stopped at the runtime limit; raise timeout_secs (up to 3600) or make the script faster. handsd refused to run it. The file must be executable, owned by root and not writable by group or others, and so must its directory. There is no script unit then; the reason is in the handsd journal as handsd: script <name> refused: .... systemd-run could not start the unit. Only script <name> failed appears in the handsd journal and there is no unit log. Run the script by hand to see whether it starts at all. Reproduce it by hand with the same variable handsd sets:
sudo SERVER_HANDS_TRIGGER=manual /etc/server-hands/scripts/media.shYour shell’s environment is richer than the transient unit’s, so a failure that only happens under handsd is usually a missing PATH entry or HOME. Put set -x at the top of the script to log every command to the journal.
A script that is refused with “needs the drives unlocked first” has requires_unlock = true (the default); see the script options above. A protected script that the app cannot approve is covered by biometric_protection: after a biometrics change run sudo handsctl reset-approval-key <device-id>.

title: Homelab setup

content:
The GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/deb.yml) builds the package in a Debian 13 container on every push and pull request and uploads it as a workflow artifact (server-hands-deb, plus SHA256SUMS; hands-client-linux-amd64 is the test client). Pushing a tag v* (for example v0.5.0) additionally publishes the package to a signed apt repository served from GitHub Pages, so the server can install and upgrade it with plain apt.
Install on the server sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://mblcdr.github.io/Server-Hands/server-hands.gpg | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/server-hands.gpg >/dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/server-hands.gpg] https://mblcdr.github.io/Server-Hands/ ./" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/server-hands.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install server-handsLater updates are sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade. The package never enables the service by itself (see the setup guide), and upgrades keep /etc/server-hands/config.toml (it is a conffile).
Before trusting the key, compare its fingerprint with the one you recorded when you generated it: gpg --show-keys --with-fingerprint /etc/apt/keyrings/server-hands.gpg. The key is fetched over HTTPS from the same host as the packages, so the fingerprint check is what protects the first install.
One-time setup (repository owner) Signing key. A dedicated key used only for this repository: export GNUPGHOME=$(mktemp -d) gpg --batch --passphrase '' --quick-generate-key "Server Hands apt <you@example.com>" ed25519 sign 5y gpg --list-keys --with-fingerprint # write the fingerprint down (README, password manager) gpg --armor --export-secret-keys "Server Hands apt" > /tmp/apt-signing-key.ascStore the private key only as a repository secret, then delete the file and the temporary GNUPGHOME. Secrets (GitHub: Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions): APT_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY = the contents of apt-signing-key.asc. Add APT_GPG_PASSPHRASE only if you gave the key a passphrase. Pages. Settings, Pages, Source: “Deploy from a branch”, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). The branch is created by the first publish; if the Pages setting is not selectable yet, run step 4 first and then set it. First release. git tag v0.5.0 && git push origin v0.5.0. Wait for the publish job, then open https://mblcdr.github.io/Server-Hands/. The tag name becomes the package version (v0.5.0 gives 0.5.0), so tag in increasing order; apt only upgrades to a higher version. Builds from main get versions like 0.5.0+git42.abc1234 and are artifacts only, never published unless you run the workflow manually with “publish” ticked.
Rotating the key: generate a new one, update the secret, publish a release, and tell users to replace /etc/apt/keyrings/server-hands.gpg. The key expires after five years as created above; extend it with gpg --quick-set-expire before then and update the secret.
Notes amd64 only. An arm64 build needs a second job on an ubuntu-24.04-arm runner (free for public repositories). Third-party actions are referenced by major version tag. Pin them to commit SHAs if you want protection against a compromised tag; the publish job holds the signing key, so that is the part worth pinning first. The repository is “flat” (deb ... ./), so there is no dists/ tree and no codename to choose.

Pushing a tag v* (for example v0.5.0) additionally publishes the package to a signed apt repository served from GitHub Pages, so the server can install and upgrade it with plain apt.
title: Apt repository

content:
The app workflow (.github/workflows/app.yml) tests the app and builds an APK on every push and pull request. On a tag vX.Y.Z it builds a signed release APK and attaches it, with SHA256SUMS, to the GitHub Release of that tag (created if missing). The same tag also drives the server package (deb workflow), so one tag releases both. The tag sets versionName (v0.5.0 gives 0.5.0) and versionCode (major*10000 + minor*100 + patch, e.g. 500).
Without the signing secrets the workflow still builds a debug APK as an artifact (fine for tests, not for release); a tag build without them fails on purpose.
One-time: create the release key Do this on your own machine and keep the file safe. If you lose it, or the password, you can never publish an update that installs over the old app (Android requires the same signing key; users would have to uninstall, which destroys their pairing and vault).
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore server-hands-release.jks -alias serverhands \ -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 10000keytool asks for a keystore password and certificate details (the name can be anything). Press Enter at “key password” to reuse the keystore password. Then record the SHA-256 fingerprint to compare later:
keytool -list -v -keystore server-hands-release.jks -alias serverhands | grep SHA256Back the .jks file and the password up somewhere that is not this repository (password manager, encrypted backup). Never commit it.
One-time: add the repository secrets GitHub: repository, Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, New repository secret. Add four secrets:
Secret Value ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64 the keystore file, base64 encoded: macOS base64 -i server-hands-release.jks | pbcopy, Linux base64 -w0 server-hands-release.jks ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD the keystore password ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS serverhands (or the alias you used) ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD the key password; same as the keystore password if you pressed Enter With the GitHub CLI instead: gh secret set ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64 < <(base64 -i server-hands-release.jks) and gh secret set ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD, and so on.
Secrets are not passed to pull requests from forks, so those builds are debug APKs.
Release git tag v0.5.0 && git push origin v0.5.0The workflow prints the signer certificate SHA-256; it must match the fingerprint you recorded. Download server-hands_0.5.0.apk from the release (check it against SHA256SUMS) and install it with adb install -r, or open it on the phone.
Local release builds cd app export JAVA_HOME=/opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk@17 SERVERHANDS_KEYSTORE=/path/to/server-hands-release.jks SERVERHANDS_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD=... SERVERHANDS_KEY_ALIAS=serverhands \ ./gradlew :androidApp:assembleRelease -PversionName=0.5.0 -PversionCode=500Without those variables assembleRelease produces an unsigned APK that Android will not install.
Code shrinking (R8) Release builds are minified and resource-shrunk (about 31 MB before, 3.4 MB after); no keep rules are needed (app/androidApp/proguard-rules.pro). The app has no reflection of its own, BouncyCastle’s lightweight API is called directly and kotlinx.serialization ships its own rules.
To check a change did not break that, run the instrumented tests against a shrunk and obfuscated debug build on an emulator (release builds refuse software keys, so they cannot run there):
cd app ./gradlew :androidApp:connectedDebugAndroidTest -PminifyDebug=true \ -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.pairing="$(head -1 /tmp/fake.out | base64 | tr -d '\n')"(start the fake server as in app/README.md; its pairing token is single-use, so restart it for every run). proguard-verify.pro only applies to this mode: it keeps the Kotlin stdlib, kotlinx JSON and the crypto package that the test APK borrows from the app.
Not covered by those tests: the Compose screens, the QR scanner and the real biometric prompt. Check those on a phone with the signed release APK.
Builds are not reproducible yet (Phase 5).
summary: The app workflow (.github/workflows/app.yml) tests the app and builds an APK on every push and pull request. title: Android app release

content:
Single version, no negotiation, no fallback. Anything else is rejected.
Keys Key Algorithm Where Purpose Server identity S Ed25519 /var/lib/server-hands/identity.key (0600, root) signs every server message; pinned by clients Server TLS key ECDSA P-256 self-signed cert state dir transport only; SPKI SHA-256 pinned by clients Request ephemeral E X25519 RAM only, one per request HPKE recipient key; destroyed after approval Device identity D ECDSA P-256 Android Keystore (StrongBox preferred), non-exportable, setUnlockedDeviceRequired signs approvals; public key stored on server at pairing Approval key A ECDSA P-256 Android Keystore (StrongBox preferred), non-exportable, per-use strong biometric (setUserAuthenticationRequired, timeout 0, invalidated by new enrolment) signs script approvals; public key registered on the server, one per device Vault key AES-256-GCM Android Keystore, per-use biometric encrypts the passphrase vault blob Primitives: HPKE RFC 9180 base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305. Hash: SHA-256. Randomness: OS CSPRNG.
Encoding Messages are JSON. Signed messages use an envelope { "body": "<base64url of exact body bytes>", "sig": "<base64url>" }. Signatures cover domain_label || 0x00 || body_bytes. Verifiers parse the body only after the signature verifies. No canonicalization is needed because the signed bytes are transmitted verbatim.
Domain labels: hands/v1/server-reply, hands/v1/device-request, hands/v1/approve, hands/v1/pair, hands/v1/script-approve.
Pairing Operator runs sudo handsctl pair over SSH. Server creates a 32-byte one-time token (expires in 5 minutes, usable once, rate-limited) and prints a QR for hands://pair?v=1&host=<ip-or-name>&port=<p>&spki=<b64url sha256>&sid=<b64url Ed25519 pub>&tok=<b64url 32B>. App scans the QR (in-app scanner only; the hands:// scheme is not registered as a deep link). It connects with TLS pinned to spki. App generates D and sends POST /v1/pair { tok, device_pub, device_name }. Both sides compute SAS = decimal6(SHA-256("hands/v1/sas" || sid || device_pub || tok)). The server console and the phone display it; the operator confirms they match in handsctl pair (which blocks on confirmation). On confirmation the server stores device_id = SHA-256(device_pub)[0..16], device_pub, name, created_at, replies with a signed ack. The token is burned. App stores {server_id (hash of S), S, spki, host, name} and then, after BiometricPrompt + Keystore key creation, the vault entries for each drive (LUKS UUID + passphrase). Request lifecycle The server creates a request per boot (all locked, non-crypttab containers): req_id (16 random bytes), created_at, expires_at (+10 min), list of {luks_uuid, label, size}, E_pub.
POST /v1/requests/list Client body (signed by D, label hands/v1/device-request): { device_id, client_nonce (32B), ts }.
The body is parsed once, only to read device_id and pick the verification key; its values are used only after the signature verifies. Server verifies device is paired, |now - ts| < 120 s, and returns an envelope signed by S (label hands/v1/server-reply): { client_nonce, server_time, requests: [ { req_id, expires_at, drives: [...], e_pub, status } ] }.
The app verifies the signature against pinned S, checks client_nonce matches, checks server_time is close to its clock, and only then trusts anything in the reply.
POST /v1/requests/{req_id}/approve The app:
Re-verifies the latest list reply for this req_id (fresh nonce, not older than 60 s). Shows server name, key fingerprint and drive labels, then the BiometricPrompt (CryptoObject) decrypts the vault blob. Builds the binary plaintext (see “Normative encodings”) for the selected drives only. info and aad as defined in “Normative encodings”. (enc, ct) = HPKE.Seal(E_pub, info, aad, plaintext); zeroes plaintext and passphrases. Signs the approve message (see below) with D and POSTs { device_id, client_nonce, uuids, enc, ct, sig }. uuids are the hyphenated LUKS UUIDs in strictly ascending order; the server turns them into the AAD, so any mismatch with what was sealed fails the HPKE open. The server:
Looks up the request (must be pending, unexpired), device (paired), checks client_nonce was one it issued within the last 120 s and not yet used. Verifies the device signature, then HPKE.Open with E_priv; immediately marks the request consumed and zeroizes E_priv whether or not the unlock succeeds. Hands each (uuid, passphrase) to the unlock child over a pipe (never argv/env/file), zeroizes on completion. Replies (signed by S) per drive { luks_uuid, result: ok | bad_passphrase | already_open | error_code }. No passphrase or key material is ever echoed. For bad_passphrase, creates a new request (fresh req_id, fresh E) so the app retries. After 5 failures per device in 10 minutes, back off 5 minutes. Wire bodies (Phase 2, implemented in hands-proto::wire) All JSON, unknown fields rejected, binary fields base64url (no padding), device_id and req_id are the raw 16 bytes in base64url.
POST /v1/pair {tok, device_pub (SPKI DER), device_name}. The request blocks (up to 5 min) while the operator compares the SAS in handsctl pair; the reply is a server-signed (hands/v1/pair) {device_id, server_time}. The token is burned the moment a correct one is presented; 5 wrong tokens burn it too. POST /v1/requests/list: device-signed Envelope in, server-signed Envelope of {client_nonce, server_time, requests:[{req_id, expires_at, drives, e_pub, status}]} out. POST /v1/requests/{req_id}/approve: see above; reply is server-signed {client_nonce, req_id, results:[{luks_uuid, result}]}. POST /v1/scripts/list: device-signed Envelope of the same {device_id, client_nonce, ts} body as requests/list (same domain; the nonce is single-use, so a captured envelope cannot be replayed at either endpoint). Reply: server-signed {client_nonce, server_time, unlocked, scripts:[{name, label, mode: auto|manual, state: idle|queued|running|ok|failed, finished_at, requires_confirmation, biometric_protection}]}. requires_confirmation is a hint for the app (ask “Run X?” first; skipped when biometric_protection is set, because the biometric prompt is the confirmation). biometric_protection is enforced by the server, see below. POST /v1/scripts/run: device-signed Envelope of {device_id, client_nonce, ts, script} (unknown fields are rejected, so it cannot be confused with a list body). script is a name from the server’s config; the phone never sends a path or arguments. Refused with not_unlocked until every drive is unlocked (only for scripts whose config has requires_unlock = true, the default), busy if already queued or running, unknown_script. Reply: server-signed {client_nonce, script, state}; the script runs in the background and the outcome is read with scripts/list. POST /v1/status: device-signed Envelope of the same {device_id, client_nonce, ts} body as requests/list. Reply: server-signed {client_nonce, server_time, hostname, kernel, uptime_secs, load:[1m,5m,15m], cpus, cpu_percent, mem_total, mem_available, swap_total, swap_free, drives:[{luks_uuid, label, state: absent|locked|open|mounted, size, total, used, avail}], pools:[{name, mount_point, fstype, mounted, total, used, avail}]}. Memory and disk sizes are bytes. cpu_percent is the busy share since the previous status call (calls less than a second apart reuse the last value; the first call samples twice, 250 ms apart). drives are the configured drives; total/used/avail are the mounted filesystem’s, 0 unless mounted. pools are the post_unlock.mount_units (for example the mergerfs pool). Read-only, no secrets. POST /v1/device/approval-key: device-signed Envelope of {device_id, client_nonce, ts, approval_pub} (SPKI DER of A). The server keeps the first key it sees for the device; the same key again is accepted, a different one is refused with conflict until the operator runs handsctl reset-approval-key (re-pairing also clears it). Reply: server-signed {client_nonce}. POST /v1/scripts/challenge: device-signed Envelope of {device_id, client_nonce, ts, challenge_for} (a different field name than scripts/run, so the two bodies cannot be confused). Only for scripts with biometric_protection; approval_required if no approval key is registered, not_unlocked if the script needs unlocked drives and they are not (so the user is not asked for a biometric in vain). Reply: server-signed {client_nonce, script, challenge (32 random bytes), expires_at}. The challenge lives 60 s in RAM, is bound to this device and script, replaces any earlier one for the same pair, and is burned by the first run attempt that uses it, valid or not. POST /v1/scripts/run for a biometric_protection script also carries challenge and approval_sig in the signed body. approval_sig is A’s ECDSA signature (after a biometric, via a BiometricPrompt CryptoObject) over hands/v1/script-approve || 0x00 || lp(server_pub, device_id, script, challenge). Missing, unknown, expired or already used challenge: approval_required / expired; bad signature: unauthorized. The server cannot see the biometric itself: it knows that someone held a key that the app created as biometric-bound. It does not verify Android key attestation (planned). Error HTTP status: 400 bad_request, 401 unauthorized, 403 approval_required, 404 unknown_script, 409 replayed / busy / not_unlocked / conflict, 410 expired, 429 rate_limited, 500 internal. TLS 1.3 only, self-signed P-256 certificate (CN server-hands; Java/Android reject an empty subject DN); clients pin the SHA-256 of its SubjectPublicKeyInfo. Errors Constant-shape error bodies: { "error": "<code>" }, codes: unauthorized, expired, replayed, bad_request, rate_limited, unknown_script, busy, not_unlocked, approval_required, conflict, internal. No detail that distinguishes “unknown device” from “bad signature”.
Rules the implementations must enforce Passphrases only ever exist as raw bytes in Zeroizing/ByteArray containers; no string conversion, no logging, no panics with payload in the message, no Debug on secret types. Reject unknown JSON fields in signed bodies; reject duplicate uuid entries. Constant-time comparison for tokens, hashes and nonces. Server key change on the client = hard failure; only a fresh QR pairing recovers. The unlock child receives secrets over a pipe, runs with mlockall, PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, and a cgroup memory cap sized for argon2id (1.5 GiB headroom). Test vectors protocol/vectors/*.json: fixed keys and nonces with expected envelopes, HPKE enc/ct, and signature bytes. Rust and Kotlin both run them. Negative vectors: replayed nonce, wrong server key, wrong info fields, truncated ct, expired request, unknown device, swapped req_id.
Normative encodings (implemented in hands-proto, covered by protocol/vectors/v1.json) lp(f1, f2, ...) = concatenation of u32be(len(fi)) || fi. b64 = base64url without padding. Vectors use hex for raw bytes. Signed bytes: domain_label || 0x00 || body. Server signature: Ed25519 (RFC 8032), raw 64 bytes, verified strictly (no malleable encodings). Server public key: raw 32 bytes. Device signature: ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256, DER-encoded (what Android Signature("SHA256withECDSA") emits). Device public key: X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER (PublicKey.getEncoded()). device_id = SHA-256(spki)[0..16]. HPKE: RFC 9180 base mode, KEM 0x0020 DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), KDF 0x0001 HKDF-SHA256, AEAD 0x0003 ChaCha20-Poly1305. enc = 32 bytes; ct = ciphertext || 16-byte tag. Single-shot seal/open, empty exporter context. info = lp("hands/v1/hpke", SHA-256(S_pub), req_id, client_nonce, device_id). aad = lp(uuid_1, ..., uuid_n) with raw 16-byte LUKS UUIDs in strictly ascending order (no duplicates). Approve message (what D signs) = signed_bytes("hands/v1/approve", lp(req_id, client_nonce, enc, SHA-256(ct), aad)). Plaintext: 0x01 || count(u8) || count x (uuid[16] || len(u16be) || passphrase bytes) || zero padding to a multiple of 256 bytes. Count 1..=32, passphrase length 1..=1024, UUIDs strictly ascending, padding must be all zero, anything else is rejected. Binary (not JSON) so a passphrase never has to pass through a string type. SAS = u32be(SHA-256("hands/v1/sas" || lp(S_pub, device_spki, token))[0..4]) mod 10^6, zero-padded to 6 digits. All verification failures collapse to one opaque error; no decoder reports why it failed.
summary:
Single version, no negotiation, no fallback. Anything else is rejected.

Keys

Key Algorithm Where Purpose
Server identity S Ed25519 /var/lib/server-hands/identity.key (0600, root) signs every server message; pinned by clients
Server TLS key ECDSA P-256 self-signed cert state dir transport only; SPKI SHA-256 pinned by clients
Request ephemeral E X25519 RAM only, one per request HPKE recipient key; destroyed after approval
Device identity D ECDSA P-256 Android Keystore (StrongBox preferred), non-exportable, setUnlockedDeviceRequired signs approvals; public key stored on server at pairing
Approval key A ECDSA P-256 Android Keystore (StrongBox preferred), non-exportable, per-use strong biometric (setUserAuthenticationRequired, timeout 0, invalidated by new enrolment) signs script approvals; public key registered on the server, one per device
Vault key AES-256-GCM Android Keystore, per-use biometric encrypts the passphrase vault blob

Primitives: HPKE RFC 9180 base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305. Hash: SHA-256. Randomness: OS CSPRNG.
title: Protocol v1

content:
Assets: LUKS passphrases (phone vault, in flight, server RAM during unlock); server identity key; paired-device list.
# Threat Mitigation T1 Attacker on LAN impersonates server (ARP/DNS spoof, rogue AP, replayed old replies) QR out-of-band trust root; pinned TLS SPKI + pinned Ed25519 identity; fresh client nonce in every signed reply; no TOFU after pairing; no address from mDNS/intents/push T2 Fake server asks for other drives’ passphrases Vault releases only UUIDs recorded for that server; HPKE info binds server key, req, nonce, device T3 Network eavesdropper TLS plus independent HPKE to a per-request ephemeral key (forward secret) T4 Stolen/unlocked phone Per-use BiometricPrompt + CryptoObject, BIOMETRIC_STRONG only, key invalidated on new enrollment; revoke device + kill phone keyslot T5 Malware on phone Keystore/StrongBox non-exportable keys; passphrases in memory only briefly as zeroed ByteArray; FLAG_SECURE; no backups; overlay protection; no accessibility-visible passphrase text T6 Secrets leaking via logs/ps/core/swap on server libcryptsetup (no argv), pipes not files, Secret newtypes, no body logging, LimitCORE=0, PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, MemorySwapMax=0, mlockall (swap is unencrypted) T7 Replay of a recorded approve Single-use nonce, request consumed on first decrypt, ephemeral key destroyed, 10-min expiry T8 Brute force on approve endpoint Device-signed requests only, rate limit/backoff, constant-shape errors T9 Rogue pairing One-time 5-min token, QR only via SSH console, SAS confirmed by operator T10 Server host compromise (root) Out of scope: root can read the passphrase during unlock. Limit blast radius with a dedicated phone keyslot T11 Supply chain Signed releases, cargo-deny, pinned Gradle dependency verification, SBOM, reproducible builds T12 Phone (or a stolen paired key) used to run arbitrary commands via post-unlock scripts The phone only names a script from the server’s config, never a path or arguments; scripts must be root-owned and not group/world-writable (checked before every run); run requests are device-signed with single-use nonces; scripts only start once all drives are unlocked unless the script sets requires_unlock = false T13 Someone with the unlocked phone runs a dangerous script (for example a reboot) with one tap Per script: requires_confirmation (app dialog, convenience only) and biometric_protection (server enforced: the run needs a signature from a Keystore key that needs a fresh strong biometric, over a single-use 60 s challenge the server issued for that device and script; no replay, no reuse for another script, no pre-signing). The approval key is registered once and cannot be swapped by the phone; the operator resets it. Limit: the server trusts the app to have created the key as biometric-bound (no attestation check yet), so a rooted phone or modified app is out of scope T14 Machine details (hostname, uptime, load, memory, disk usage) leak to someone on the LAN /v1/status is a device-signed request, so only paired phones get an answer, and the reply travels inside pinned TLS. It is read-only and carries no secrets. To read the global /proc files handsd runs without ProcSubset=pid (other processes stay hidden with ProtectProc=invisible)
